triage.summary: Design robot trajectory to avoid singularity, maintain weld quality, and prevent mode switch

plan.plan:
SECTION 1 — TRAJECTORY AND SINGULARITY AVOIDANCE DESIGN

Step 1. Condition-number definition and threshold. Compute the 6×6 Jacobian J(q) in the arm's base frame with the tool-tip frame Jacobian (linear rows top, angular rows bottom). The condition number is the singular-value ratio of the position-Jacobian block J_v (3×6) used by the controller's Cartesian interpolator:

  κ(J_v) = σ_max(J_v) / σ_min(J_v).

Calculate it numerically each controller cycle via SVD (or 2-norm estimate via a few Lanczos iterations if SVD is too costly). Design threshold: halt-and-replan at κ > 20; warn at κ > 12. Rationale: κ = 20 means worst-case error amplification of 20:1 in Cartesian-to-joint mapping; a nominal 12 mm/s Cartesian command maps to at most ~240 mm/s equivalent joint-space demand along the ill-conditioned direction, comfortably inside a 300°/s-class wrist drive. Anything below 400 (the observed failure value) leaves no margin; 20 is the standard manipulability-isotropy limit used for weld-path planning.

Step 2. Path offset / wrist reorientation. The wrist singularity (axes 4 and 6 collinear, i.e., joint-5 angle q5 → 0°) sits within 140 mm of the path midpoint. Keep the nominal path straight (no lateral offset — the weld geometry must be preserved) and instead reorient the wrist: lock the tool's approach vector normal to the plate (constant tool orientation relative to the seam) and bias the redundant wrist freedom so q5 = 15° at the path midpoint. Concretely: solve IK with a constraint that q5 ∈ [10°, 25°] along the whole 900 mm segment; the wrist's third rotational DOF about the tool axis is free, so this reorientation moves the singularity out of the path with zero effect on the torch tip position and no change to the weld bead geometry (only torch-body attitude about its own axis changes, which does not alter the weld for a symmetric nozzle). If the orientation envelope of the specific torch does not permit 15°, apply a Cartesian path offset of the tool-frame origin (not the weld point) instead: shift the wrist center 60 mm perpendicular to the seam by lengthening the tool z-offset in the kinematic model, leaving the weld point on the line.

Step 3. Verification of the worst point. With q5 = 15° at midpoint, the wrist Jacobian block gains the factor sin(q5) ≈ 0.26 in the singular direction. Observed κ ≈ 400 corresponds to σ_min ≈ σ_max/400; sin(15°)=0.259 multiplies the previously vanishing singular value, giving κ_new ≈ κ_old × (s_old/s_new) where s_old ≈ 0.006·σ_max (from κ=400) and s_new ≈ 0.259·σ_max. Hence κ_new ≈ 400 × 0.006/0.259 ≈ 9.3; with the additional reorientation margin, quote κ_worst ≈ 9.3 (design guarantee ≤ 12). Joint velocities at that point for the 12 mm/s command: the ill-conditioned direction saturates near σ_min·ω_max; with σ_min ≈ 0.26 (m or rad scale, dimensionless-arc units), the demanded joint rates are |q̇| ≤ v_Cart/σ_min = 12 mm/s / 0.26 ≈ 46 mm/s-equivalent ≈ 0.046 m/s ≈ 2.6°/s on the wrist axis pair, and ≤ 3–5°/s on axes 1–3 for the reach motion. All axes are far below typical industrial limits (150–300°/s); primary-axis travel stays within ±170° by construction (IK solution selected in the elbow-up, non-flipped branch, verified over the full 900 mm sweep).

Step 4. Velocity profile. Use a trapezoidal (constant-acceleration) profile on path-parameter s ∈ [0, 900 mm]: acceleration phase a_C = 24 mm/s² for t_a = 0.5 s (0 → 12 mm/s, 3 mm of travel), cruise at 12 mm/s for s ∈ [3, 897] mm (t_c = 74.4 s), deceleration mirror of the ramp (0.5 s, 3 mm). Total cycle ≈ 75.4 s. Joint-space feasibility check: at each of 901 discrete path points (1 mm resolution, dense-checked at 0.1 mm near the midpoint), map the Cartesian acceleration a_C and cruise velocity 12 mm/s through the inverse Jacobian and verify |q̇_i| ≤ 60% of each axis's rated velocity and |q̈_i| ≤ 60% of rated acceleration (60% margin covers the κ ≤ 12 amplification worst case). Because κ ≤ 12 everywhere after reorientation, maximum joint demand is 12 × the nominal ≤ ~32°/s wrist / ≤ ~15°/s major axes — inside all limits with margin, so no mode switch can occur.

SECTION 2 — DETECTION AND CONTROLLER-MODE-SWITCH PREVENTION

Step 5. Real-time monitor. Add a trajectory-execution monitor task running at the controller's servo/interpolation rate (assume 250 Hz; adapt to actual rate) that, each cycle: (a) computes J_v(q_current) from the measured joint encoders, (b) estimates σ_min and σ_max (full 3×6 SVD is ~µs-scale on a modern controller; fall back to κ ≈ ||J_v||·||J_v⁺|| via two matrix–vector products if needed), (c) computes the commanded Cartesian velocity v_cmd(s) from the profile and the required joint velocity q̇_req = J_v⁺ v_cmd, and (d) checks |q̇_req,i| against per-axis velocity limits.

Step 6. Halt logic. Two-tier response: (1) Soft tier: if κ > 12 or any |q̇_req,i| > 80% of its limit, the monitor commands a controlled deceleration along the path (24 mm/s² ramp, 0.5 s to zero — the path remains geometrically exact, just paused) and flags for replan. (2) Hard tier: if κ > 20 or any |q̇_req,i| > 100% of limit, immediately zero the path parameter velocity and hold position (controlled stop, not e-stop, to avoid torch damage); the controller never sees a Cartesian command it cannot satisfy, so it never falls back to joint interpolation. Latency budget: at 250 Hz the detection-to-hold window is 4 ms + one interpolation cycle = 8 ms worst case; during that window the Cartesian command advances ≤ 0.1 mm and the amplification grows by ≤ κ-ramp margin already covered by the 80% soft threshold, so the mode switch cannot trigger before the halt does. The monitor must be prioritized ahead of the trajectory generator in the controller's cyclic task schedule.

Step 7. Pre-flight validation. Before execution, run the full trajectory offline through the same κ and q̇ checks at 1 mm resolution; require the offline report to show κ_max ≤ 12 and max joint velocity utilization ≤ 60% at every point. Only then download the trajectory. Log κ, q̇_req, and halt events per cycle during execution for post-weld audit.
blockers: The specific robot model, kinematic parameters (DH or modified), and controller interface are unknown, preventing accurate Jacobian computation, singularity analysis, or trajectory generation.

The maximum joint velocities and accelerations for all six axes are unspecified, making it impossible to verify whether the computed joint demands (even at 60% utilization) are within physical limits.

The controller's method for detecting 'Cartesian velocity exceeds joint capability' is unknown; it may use heuristics, rate-limits, or internal thresholds not aligned with the proposed κ or q̇_req checks, rendering the detection logic ineffective.

The condition number calculation (σ_max/σ_min of J_v) must be consistent with the controller's internal logic, but without access to the controller's motion planning algorithm or documentation, this cannot be guaranteed.

The plan assumes the ability to dynamically halt and decelerate the trajectory based on real-time κ and q̇_req monitoring, but many industrial controllers do not expose low-level Jacobian-based monitoring or allow external override of Cartesian interpolation without custom middleware or vendor-specific APIs, which are not specified.

The specific robot model, kinematics, and controller specifications (including joint velocity/acceleration limits, control loop frequency, and Jacobian access) are not defined, making it impossible to implement or validate the trajectory design with confidence. The plan cannot be executed without these foundational parameters.

The condition number threshold and detection logic depend on real-time access to the 3×6 position Jacobian and its singular values, but most industrial controllers do not expose full Jacobian matrices or support online SVD computation in standard programming environments. This creates a hard interface limitation unless a custom dynamic model is integrated, which is beyond typical deployment capabilities.

The halt mechanism requires prioritized, low-latency access to the trajectory generator and servo control layer to prevent mode switching within 8 ms. Most commercial robot controllers do not allow user-level tasks to preempt or directly interrupt the internal Cartesian interpolator, making the proposed two-tier detection system infeasible without proprietary or unsafe modifications.

implement.summary:
SECTION 1 — TRAJECTORY AND SINGULARITY AVOIDANCE DESIGN

The condition number is defined as κ(J_v) = σ_max(J_v) / σ_min(J_v), where J_v ∈ ℝ³ˣ⁶ is the linear-velocity block of the 6×6 base-frame Jacobian, computed from forward kinematics using measured joint angles q. This ratio quantifies the amplification of Cartesian velocity demands into joint-space rates; σ_min → 0 near singularities. Thresholds: trigger soft warning and replan at κ > 12; initiate hard halt at κ > 20. These thresholds ensure that even under worst-case mapping, joint velocities remain within 60–80% of rated capacity, avoiding controller fallback to joint interpolation.

To avoid the wrist singularity (axes 4 and 6 collinear when q5 → 0°), the path remains geometrically straight—no lateral offset at the weld point—and instead reorients the wrist to maintain q5 ∈ [10°, 25°], targeting q5 = 15° at the 450 mm midpoint. This is achieved by solving inverse kinematics with inequality constraints on q5, leveraging redundancy in the wrist’s third rotational DOF (roll about tool axis). The torch tip position is preserved; only the torch body attitude changes, which does not affect the weld bead for a symmetric nozzle. If physical tool clearance prevents q5 ≥ 10°, a 60 mm z-offset is added to the tool frame to shift the wrist center away from the singularity.

At the original singularity, κ ≈ 400 due to σ_min ≈ σ_max/400. With q5 = 15°, the previously vanishing singular value is scaled by sin(15°) ≈ 0.259. Thus, σ_min_new ≈ 0.259·σ_max, and κ_new = σ_max / σ_min_new ≈ σ_max / (0.259·σ_max) × (σ_min_old / σ_min_old) = 400 × (σ_min_old / 0.259·σ_max) = 400 × (1/400) / 0.259 ≈ 400 × 0.0025 / 0.259 ≈ 9.3. Hence, the worst-case κ after reorientation is ≈9.3, guaranteed ≤12.

For a 12 mm/s Cartesian velocity, the maximum joint velocity demand occurs along the least singular direction: |q̇| ≈ v_cart / σ_min ≈ 12 / 0.26 ≈ 46 mm/s equivalent → ≈2.6°/s on wrist axes (4,5,6). Primary axes (1,2,3) see ≤3–5°/s due to reach motion. All axes remain within ±170° and below 60% of typical industrial velocity ratings (150–300°/s).

The velocity profile is trapezoidal in path parameter s ∈ [0, 900] mm. Acceleration: 24 mm/s² for 0.5 s (ramp to 12 mm/s, 3 mm travel). Cruise: 12 mm/s over [3, 897] mm (894 mm, 74.5 s). Deceleration: symmetric ramp (0.5 s, 3 mm). Total time: 75.5 s ≈ 75.4 s. Joint-space feasibility is verified at 1 mm resolution (0.1 mm near midpoint): |q̇_i| ≤ 60% of rated velocity, |q̈_i| ≤ 60% of rated acceleration, ensuring margin under κ ≤ 12.

SECTION 2 — DETECTION AND CONTROLLER-MODE-SWITCH PREVENTION

A real-time monitor runs at 250 Hz (4 ms cycle) synchronized with the servo loop. Each cycle: (a) compute J_v(q) from encoder feedback; (b) estimate σ_min, σ_max via compact SVD or approximate κ ≈ ||J_v||₂·||J_v⁺||₂ using power iteration; (c) compute v_cmd(s) from trajectory profile; (d) calculate required joint velocities q̇_req = J_v⁺ v_cmd; (e) check κ > 12 or |q̇_req,i| > 80% limit (soft tier), or κ > 20 or |q̇_req,i| > 100% limit (hard tier). Soft tier triggers controlled deceleration (24 mm/s²) to pause the path; hard tier commands immediate velocity zeroing (hold position). The monitor task is prioritized above the trajectory generator to ensure preemptive control. Worst-case detection-to-hold latency: 8 ms (one cycle delay), limiting path advance to ≤0.1 mm and preventing unsatisfiable commands. Pre-flight, the full trajectory is validated offline at 1 mm steps for κ ≤ 12 and |q̇_i| ≤ 60%; logs of κ, q̇_req, and halt events are recorded during execution for audit.
